claims.text: A strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys originates from magnetoelastic coupling.
High configurational or chemical disorder generates local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions enhance magnetoelastic coupling.
Local distortions facilitate a field-induced reorientation or subtle phase change between competing magnetic states.
Field-induced evolution from a disordered paramagnetic state toward a weak ferromagnetic state can produce a large magnetic entropy change.
A chemically disordered matrix preserves rapid heat exchange through coherent pathways.
The disordered matrix preserves mechanical stability and low hysteresis.
A single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloy based on 3d transition metals is a realizable initial material state.
The proposed initial state near but below the Curie temperature has minimal pre-existing long-range order.
Slight changes in transition-metal mixing ratios or heat treatment can controllably increase or decrease local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions and nanoscale chemical heterogeneities modify magnetic exchange interactions.
An applied magnetic field triggers magnetic-moment reorientation or magnetostructural fluctuations that are amplified by local distortions.
Structural disorder minimizes hysteresis by stabilizing phases and smoothing magnetic transitions.
A coherent structure ensures rapid heat conduction while maintaining mechanical stability.
Alloys with optimized, higher local lattice distortion will show larger low-field adiabatic temperature changes and isothermal entropy changes than reduced-distortion controls.
Increasing local distortion can improve the magnetocaloric response without compromising thermal conductivity, hysteresis, or mechanical stability.
A reduced-distortion control may exhibit higher magnetic hysteresis than the enhanced-distortion material.

The proposed mechanism should apply near the magnetic transition under fields below 1 T in single-phase 3d-transition-metal high-entropy alloys, but may fail when first-order transformations, secondary phases, or excessive brittleness occur.
